speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: IEA analysis shows that annual energy intensity improvements need to rise immediately to at least 2.6% in a trajectory consistent with our climate goals." I would like to ask the Minister how is our performance in industrial energy efficiency efforts compared with other countries?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What is the feedback from industries on the obstacles they are facing and what can the Ministry do to address these concerns?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How are we to fulfil our commitment to the Paris Agreement?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Are there any new plans to improve on our industrial energy efficiency?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Our city state has done well in managing the air quality from vehicle emissions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Unlike the days before year 2000, certainly we hardly see smoky vehicles on our roads, except some from across the causeway.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Even the public can report to NEA if they see any smoky vehicles on our roads.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: NEA requires periodic checks for buses and diesel vehicles and we strive to reduce domestic emissions to meet the 2020 air quality targets benchmarked against WHO standards.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We have been successful and there are lessons to be learnt from what is happening in China, India and France where smoke from vehicle emissions had created havoc on the ambient air quality.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The toll can be very serious as we can see how the haze has impacted the health of the people.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: WHO has pointed out that air pollution poses one of the biggest environmental health risks, especially for heart diseases.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister update the House on what is the strategy to achieve these targets and what has been done so far to improve the air quality in Singapore?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Diesel vehicles are found to be the major culprit in polluting the air.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Diesel engines emit particulates into the air at ground level, as well as emit nitrogen oxides.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Nitrogen oxides can help form ground-level ozone, which can lead to breathing difficulties for those suffering from respiratory problems.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: At the last COS debate, we were told that a study on diesel vehicles would be undertaken by SUTD.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that it has recently submitted a report on alternative technologies to the Ministry.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share with the House the outcome of this study?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are some older commercial vehicles retained by their owners which do not meet current day emission standards.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What are the Ministry's plans to address these old commercial vehicles?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Apart from this, what are plans to curb emissions from petrol cars and motorcycles?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I would like to briefly point out that there is much that can be done to improve the waste collection system.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Frequently, we can see cleaners manually hauling refuse to the bin centres from the chutes at the HDB blocks.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This gives rise to complaints from residents about the odour and the spread of pests when this exercise is not done properly.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Are there any plans for the Ministry to improve on this waste disposal by cleaners?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I note that the cost of water supply has risen over the years and the Government is raising prices by 30% in two phases from this July.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I think what we need to do is to share with Singaporeans what the Government is doing to meet future demand and make our country resilient against any supply disruption, especially in the current uncertain weather conditions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This would, I feel, at least make the people understand and appreciate the big picture behind the price increase.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: On climate change, I would like to ask the Minister what are PUB's plans to cope with the unpredictable and intense rainfall that we may encounter in this age of weather turbulence.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I know there were drainage works carried out to alleviate flooding, but as the past months have shown, there are many pockets in our midst where more work is required.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Minister can update the House on the work done so far on the Stamford Diversion Canal, Stamford Detention Tank and the Bukit Timah First Diversion Canal.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Has any of these been completed and if so, how have they helped to prevent flooding in key areas?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: On PUB, I would like to ask if the Minister can update us on the Active, Beautiful and Clean Waters Programme which was launched a decade ago.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What more can we expect of ABC Waters for this financial year?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Recently, the NEA has designated smoking areas in busy downtown Orchard Road.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I do not know if this is after taking a cue from Nee Soon South, where we have successfully put up 42 Designated Smoking Points (DSPs) and eight more in progress; a total of 50 DSPs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Orchard Road experience is positive.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Are there other measures that we can put in place to incentivise the individual firms to be prudent and compel them to use alternative sources of energy?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With this tax, are we on track to meeting our commitment to lower carbon emissions?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Has the Ministry explored other initiatives, considering the level of carbon emitted in our day-to-day life may have compounded the problem?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, the Ministry can consider further reviewing the following.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: One, creating greater awareness of the importance of addressing climate change and its implication on Singapore and its people.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This can be done through schools, at workplaces and in public places with educational posters and documentary films, extensively promoting recycling, reducing or replacing the usage of plastics.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This can be done by providing greater access and incentives for one to exchange empty bottles for coins − a practice found in Sweden.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Pushing for consumers to bring their recyclable bags and not providing the alternative of plastic carrier bags could also be considered.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is the age-old culture that we need to reignite.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can we do more in getting electric vehicles instead of petroleum cars to ply our roads if our effort to make Singaporeans switch to public transport remains a challenge?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can we better incentivise companies and individuals to encourage such efforts?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The food we eat is what we are and what the environmental impact will be.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is important to educate Singaporeans on food that poses a negative impact on the environment. "The biggest intervention people could make towards reducing their carbon footprints is to eat significantly less red meat," said Prof Tim Benton at the University of Leeds.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: A research, led by scientists at the Oxford Martin School, found that shifting to a mostly vegetarian diet, or even simply cutting down meat consumption to within accepted health guidelines, would make a large dent in greenhouse gases.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, the eco-friendly award is a timely reminder —

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: — of what we need to do and that protecting the environment is everybody's duty.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, you have two cuts.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the beginning of this year, NEA warned that we could see an increase in the number of dengue cases towards the middle of the year.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am especially concerned about the impact of the disease on our elderly whose immune systems are weaker.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on the study of the male Aedes aegypti mosquitoes carrying the Wolbachia bacteria?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Initial studies have suggested that these released male mosquitoes have successfully mated with the urban females whose eggs do not hatch.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Does the Ministry detect a fall in the number of dengue cases in the estates where these studies were conducted?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In how many more estates will these male mosquitoes be released in the future?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The high diversity of circulating dengue serotypes is also worrying as immunity for one strain does not offer protection against other strains.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to ask how successful our public education programme on the prevention of mosquito breeding has been.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are industries and residents more aware of the dangers and being more cooperative now?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The industry sector, as the largest emitter of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, plays an important role in reducing our emissions.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Consumers can also help by using more energy-efficient appliances.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What plans does the Ministry have to improve industrial and household energy efficiency and thus reduce GHG emissions?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will these contribute towards Singapore's pledge to reduce our emissions under the Paris Agreement on climate change?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For pollutants that are carried here by the winds from neighbouring countries, what is the progress of our collaborations with these nations to cut down on activities which produce haze?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The carbon tax will affect between 30 and 40 direct emitters, such as power stations, should it start in 2019.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How much improvement in air quality resulting from this tax does the Ministry expect and will the reduction be in time for us to reach the 2020 deadline?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will the Ministry consider giving much more attractive rebates for cars which emit less pollutants to convince more buyers to switch to these cars while increasing the surcharges for more polluting vehicles?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Lastly, I hope the Ministry will look at measures to improve the quality of air in our estates by restricting indiscriminate burning for religious offerings and installing more accessible burners to encourage responsible usage.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Ministry also commission studies to improve the design of these burners?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At last year's COS, the Ministry announced that it would undertake a study on diesel vehicles.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I understand that SUTD has recently submitted its report on alternative technologies to the Ministry.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In 2016, some major cities around the world have taken actions to curb diesel vehicles which are known to emit higher levels of Particulate Matter (PM) and Nitrogen Oxides (NOx).

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope our Government will consider incentives, such as road tax exemptions and other rebates, for petrol-electric hybrid commercial vehicles or, even better, perhaps to follow in the footsteps of the above countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Singapore Air Quality Data, provided by the NEA, only measures up to PM2.5.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the particles found in vehicle emissions are 100 times smaller and thus are not currently captured in our air quality indices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also, in many cities around the world, curbside pollution along main trunk routes is included in air quality indices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should develop our own roadside index as part of our slew of air quality indices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Other than the informational function, the roadside air quality index will serve an educational purpose and as a progress tracking instrument in our fight against this specific pollution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Vehicular emission control is the ultimate solution to this problem.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But even as we make progress on this front, would the Ministry work with the relevant agencies to promote technological and design innovations to mitigate the effects of curbside pollution on bus commuters?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Recently, the experimental next-generation bus stop in Jurong made the news.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Equipped with a swing, rooftop garden, artwork, library books and broadcast screens, the bus stop makes waiting productive and may even encourage more waiting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But this is actually a dangerous proposition given curbside pollution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope such experimental bus stops would also test technologies and designs to mitigate curbside pollution.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Anyone who has crossed the causeway can see the long line of motorcycles entering and leaving Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many motorbikes entering Singapore from Malaysia for work during dawn and rush back by night, often riding fast to beat the jams.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some of these motorcycles, with modified engines and exhaust, tend to emit loud noises, which cause a nuisance.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have received several feedback from residents who stay along the PIE leading to the Tuas checkpoint about this noise pollution.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One way you we can fight climate change is by promoting the use of hybrid cars or cars with lower emission.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Ministry look into providing more incentives for buying vehicles with cleaner emissions, as well as introducing tighter emission standards for new vehicles.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ultimately, we need to make sure that hybrid cars cost cheaper, at least slightly than high emission cars, so that more people will buy them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The haze pollution in 2016 was much less severe than in 2015.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Did the Ministry's effort in naming the companies who may have contributed to the haze help?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure the Government's decision to buy only green label paper helps significantly as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, will the Government now look into procuring only sustainable palm oil, considering that it has announced support for the roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil recently?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, what are the Ministry's expectations for the haze situation in 2017?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A haze-free ASEAN is only possible if all ASEAN states work together to resolve this longstanding problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What is the progress of the Ministry's effort on the regional front to achieve a haze-free ASEAN?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Specifically, how will Singapore be working with Indonesia and assist in the effort to prevent and clamp down on forest fires?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What role can businesses and the general public play in contributing to this vision?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Its size is five times, larger than all of our 17 freshwater reservoirs combined.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: How will the water supply in Singapore be affected if Linggiu reservoir runs dry?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: How we can build our water resilience against contingencies, such as weather uncertainties and supply disruptions?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: How will our water supply be affected if Malaysia decides not to extend our water agreement?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: What plans do the Ministry and PUB have to ensure that our water supply is adequate in meeting future demand?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We have been experiencing more instances of extreme weather conditions, from prolonged dry weather to intense downpours resulting in flooding.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: More recently, we have lots of rain in the afternoons.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Is the Ministry working on a long-term infrastructural solution to collect water during the heavy rains while mitigating the problems of flooding?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: It is just as important for us to minimise water wastage.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: How efficient is our system of inspection to detect, prevent and minimise water wastage and leaks?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: For many years, most of us have taken the flow of clean water from our taps for granted.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We must step up our efforts to increase public awareness of our water conservation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: How has the progress of our public education efforts been?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Can the Minister share updates on water saving designs and installations in our buildings?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Would the Ministry elaborate on the Government's expenditure, investments and subsidies for water made to ensure sufficient and reliable water supply for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: How does the Government reach the figure of 30% for the increase of water price?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Given the current poor economic climate, businesses, in general, will find it difficult to stomach the water price increases.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Is it possible for the Ministry to defer the price increase or stagger it over the next five years with smaller annual adjustments?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: What are the plans the Ministry has to help and encourage Singaporeans to practise water conservation and adopt water saving measures at home?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: What are the available technologies families can tap on to reduce their water bills?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: However, industries that use large amounts of water, such as food, paper and chemicals, may be more adversely affected.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As water is a basic cost for these industries, this cost may then be transferred to consumers.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can the Ministry consider a "Tiered Pricing System" to help those industries which are more reliant on water?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Each person in a household may be trying their best, saving water, reducing their water consumption.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But it adds up if you have many people at home in a big household.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Progressive water taxation calculated at a per-household level does not distinguish between big or small families.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This may end up having a regressive effect on large families living in the same home at the same address, some of whom may be lower-income families.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Has the Ministry studied the possibility of per capita consumption as a new measure, if not for now, then for the future, as our technology improves?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some other agencies already consider per capita measures for forms of financial assistance and subsidy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: As a Singaporean, I am grateful for the efforts made by Minister Masagos and other Ministers and Members of Parliament, agencies and fellow Singaporeans as well, helping to clarify and give a clearer picture about this move.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: These clarifications, via parliamentary debates, media coverage and ground engagement, have given some Singaporeans an accurate picture on issues relating to water and the recent proposed initiatives to increase water tariffs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: I, myself, have attended and carried out my own engagement with my residents and fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: I realised that we need a lot of explanation, sometimes argument, and, finally, most importantly, many get the accurate picture.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: And there were a few comments made by them after the engagement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: For example, one person I met, who after speaking to him for a while, told me, "Why didn't you tell me this earlier?" Another one I met, who was very concerned about needy Singaporeans, shared with me and said that, "Fortunately, I met you this morning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: I have a better perspective about the issue now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: But you must help needy Singaporeans." And another one shared with me that he has read this post which shows that the water price will increase by more than 30%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: He said, "The social media is a dangerous place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: I got all my facts and figures wrong." So, I feel that without our efforts and clarifications, I fear that many Singaporeans will get the wrong information and may be misguided.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Still, there are residents whom I met who were concerned about the increase in water tariffs.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: I think many of my comments echo the previous Members'.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Many residents that I have spoken with understand and do support the rationale for this increase, considering the enormous sums of money that we have to continue spending on our water infrastructure in order to achieve water self-sufficiency in the long term.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: First, is it possible to perhaps stagger the increase even further, perhaps, say, 10% over three years, instead of 15% over two years?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Another question is: what are the Ministry's plans to mitigate future increases in the price of water down the road?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: It has also been reassuring to hear over the last few days in this House, the help which lower and middle income families will get to manage this increase.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Nonetheless, I am still concerned about some financially vulnerable households which may still be coping or struggling with utilities arrears, despite the subsidies.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: How will the Ministry assist this group of low-income households cope?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is also an important part of Singapore's social landscape where Singaporeans from all walks of lifes and all backgrounds come together to enjoy a good meal and at an affordable price.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must retain and strengthen this unique identity of ours and keep the culture of hawker centres alive and well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am glad that the Ministry commissioned a Hawker Centre 3.0 Committee, chaired by Senior Minister of State Amy Khor, to look into how we can make improvements to the overall offerings of hawker centres, making them more vibrant and to sustain the hawker business.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The report, with a list of recommendations, was released last month.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Are there any measures to address the cost implications of productivity initiatives on the hawkers?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thirdly, what plans does the Government have to increase the vibrancy of hawker centres?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And fourthly, NEA has been advocating tray-return with varied levels of success.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What more will the Government do to improve tray-return rates in existing centres?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Back then, NEA acknowledged that the tray return initiative had still some way to go before the practice takes root.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It has been more than four years since the return tray initiative was launched.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I am not sure if my experience and observation at hawker centres is an outlier, but the practice has not taken root and the initiative does not seem to be achieving its objective.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Tables at hawker centres and food outlets continue to be cluttered with leftover food, dishes and trays, regardless of peak or off-peak hours.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I seek an update from the Minister on the progress of the roll-out of the return tray facilities in all hawker centres and the effort NEA intends to take to make this initiative work.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Next, I wish to seek an update from NEA on its anti-littering campaigns.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Let's Bin It!" was rather a mouthful and forgettable as the message was not sustained as well.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Littering remains a problem in our city state despite the many years of effort to educate the public on the anti-social behaviour.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: As a first-world country, we are certainly not living like one in the area of cleanliness.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I urge the Ministry not to let up in its effort to imbue the public with social responsibility for the good of the country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Recently, in December 2016, NEA announced that it was moving forward with the next phase with two components.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The first component is the call for social enterprises to tender for the management of two new hawker centres at Yishun and Jurong West.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: NEA believes this would offer NTUC Foodfare economies of scale and greater flexibility to experiment with new ideas and operational processes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Concerning the "pilot group", given the geographical spread of the hawker centres, how are economies of scale achieved?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Why is there a need, in the first place, for economies of scale?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Is the operator under cost pressures and what are these?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Have rental rates at the Bedok Interchange Hawker Centre gone up in the last three years?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Similarly, have the prices of the food there gone up in the last three years?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: For the two new hawker centres in the group, will there be a mix of subsidised and non-subsidised stallholders paying market rentals?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The same question applies to the two new hawker centres being tendered out for social enterprise management.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Also, would NTUC Foodfare be excluded, in the interest of allowing for a diversity of operators, to experiment with new ideas and operational processes and to develop expertise?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: If NTUC Foodfare requires economies of scale, then what about the new operators?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: This is despite years of ongoing public education and enhanced fines for litterbugs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Will there be changes to how the CWO is conducted to increase their effectiveness?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: All of us know that it is called "killer litter".

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: But it is difficult to apprehend the culprits.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on the effectiveness of these cameras in deterring high-rise littering?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: How many cameras are in use and how many litterbugs have been caught in the last year?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can NEA provide an update on the effectiveness of the designated smoking areas and points in Orchard Road and Nee Soon South?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: What are the Government's further plans to protect the general public from the harmful effects of second-hand smoke?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Will it be moving towards only allowing smoking at designated areas, instead of having a list of prohibited areas?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Will the Ministry consider expanding the ban on smoking outside designated areas to other busy streets, such as the Central Business District and the Civic District, as done in other cities like Tokyo and Kyoto?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am encouraged by NEA's intention to implement a regulated national system to collect and recycle e-waste and would like to ask the Minister for an update about this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In the meantime, we still face the problem of appliances, such as fridges and air-conditioners which contain refrigerant gas, such as HCFCs, a gas which is extremely harmful to the environment and to human health.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It seems that, currently, there are insufficient facilities and industry incentives for proper disposal of these appliances and many are not properly discarded.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In the US, the venting of HCFCs is illegal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: And Hong Kong and Australia have also set guidelines.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I understand that NEA will phase out the import of these fridges with HCFCs by 2030.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: What facilities are currently available in Singapore for the venting of HCFCs, and has the Ministry set any industry guidelines?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Would the Ministry consider setting up a national facility for the proper removal of HCFCs from appliances before they are incinerated?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This is not a small amount for our size.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: According to a 2013 article published in the journal, Waste Management, 500 million computers became obsolete in the United States between 1997 and 2007.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: China generated 1.11 million tonnes of e-waste annually.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: While I should point out that precise comparisons are difficult because of differences in definitions and time period considered, we should not delay making strong moves to address what will certainly turn out to be a growing problem for our environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Because we have limited space and disposal options, any accumulation over time will be more difficult for us to manage later.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Also, the scale of the e-waste challenge in Asia is unclear but, by all accounts, growing, adding to the concern.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The lack of a visible nature of e-waste at present appears to suggest that the problem is obscure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: As e-waste accumulates, without a comprehensive management scheme, the problem, including the requirements for specialised methods of dealing with toxic materials, will grow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: A national management plan should include the capability for tracking e-waste production and address improper disposal.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: In HDB estates under my care, I frequently see cleaners manually hauling refuse to the bin centres from the chutes.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: I also get complaints from residents on the odour and pests when these activities are not done properly or when the bin centres are not properly secured.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: How does the Ministry plan to improve waste collection in our housing estates and hawker centres?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: And will the Ministry act to upgrade the older bin centres in some of our estates?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: I would also like to suggest that we improve the way that waste is disposed of in the first place.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: For example, food waste is the primary culprit for causing odour and attracting pests.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: The Eco-Wiz's EcoDigester breaks down food to produce water that can be reused for cleaning or landscaping.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: This system, as I understand it, is already installed at around 30 hotels, restaurants and schools and at the Ang Mo Kio market.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Each digester can process about one tonne of waste per day.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Can this system be studied further and, perhaps, be installed at each precinct so that we can involve residents to dispose of their food waste in an environmentally-friendly way and also generate some water along the way?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Further, the waste that is generated is more complex to process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For example, many residents replace their mobile phones or computers once every two to three years and electronic goods would come in several layers of packaging.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Could the Ministry share what it sees as key waste streams and outline its broad plans to handle the waste in the upcoming years?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As a result, the amount of refuse being burnt and buried at the Semakau landfill has been steadily increasing with the growing population and economic activity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This is not sustainable as Singapore has limited land and sea space for landfills.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Besides efforts to reduce waste, we should also look at how we could better recycle waste.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: I understand that NEA has already worked with the private sector to treat food waste, for example, in hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Many large F&B operators have also installed their own on-site food waste digesters.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: While these are commendable, these premises only treat the waste they generate.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: There are benefits to adopt a district-level approach to treat food waste from various premises, such as economies of scale and avoiding the need for individual premises to set aside space for their own digester.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Can the Minister provide an update on the project?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui, you have three cuts.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: At Our Tampines Hub, we have an Eco-digester Centre.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: From this, we are able to derive approximately 100 kg of fertilizer, 1,000 litres of non-portable water and 600 litres of liquid nutrients.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: The water is used for general cleaning of the Eco-digester centre and the nutrients are used for landscapes in our hub.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: In 2016, the Ministry announced its plans for a district-level food waste recycling pilot.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Could the Ministry give an update on its plans to promote food waste recycling on a larger scale?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: And will we involve more children in these programmes to raise their awareness of food wastage?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: The domestic recycling rates in Singapore have stagnated at around 19% to 20% for many years and our contamination rate is high.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: This is possibly because the rubbish chutes in our housing estates are so convenient.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: What is the plan to tackle this problem going forward and how can we encourage more people to recycle?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: There is much potential to improve waste collection in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: I frequently see cleaners manually moving garbage from the chutes to the bin centre.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Sometimes, we get complaints from residents about the smell and the pests when these activities are not properly carried out.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: What is the Ministry's plan to improve waste collection?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: As Singapore becomes more affluent and as our population grows, we also generate more waste.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Furthermore, waste is getting more complex to process, and many residents replace household electronic items that come in different packaging.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: How can we educate the public on better ways of disposal?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Could the Ministry share the plans to handle waste in future?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The environment has been at the top of our minds this Budget.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Many other countries are paying closer attention to the environment, even as they grow their economies.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have a plan called the Sustainable Singapore Blueprint (SSB).

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: A strong commitment to sustainability remains critical as we build our future economy.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Ms K Thanaletchimi have highlighted, it will take not only Government support but also the collective effort of every individual to realise this SSB vision.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: That is why we launched the Sustainable Singapore Movement in July last year to galvanise the community to action.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: While we stand on solid footing, the road ahead is uncertain.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: A major concern for us is climate change, a far-reaching threat that we can already see and feel today.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In recent years, our water managers, too, have had a foretaste of the looming challenge of coping with extended dry spells on the one hand and higher intensity rainfall on the other.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Singapore has to plan ahead to deal with climate change impacts.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will not only need to protect our buildings, coasts and infrastructure, but also foster greater awareness, so that we are a resilient people.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Both households and industry play a role in this, as Mr Gan Thiam Poh has noted.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We, therefore, need to focus our efforts here.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The carbon tax, however, is not a panacea for achieving our 2030 emissions pledge.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will need other measures to complement the tax.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: That is why we introduced the Energy Conservation Act (ECA) in 2013, to put in place measures, such as mandatory energy management, and encourage companies to enhance their energy efficiency.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I am pleased to report that we have made progress on this front since then.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Murata Electronics Singapore, which manufactures electronic components, is becoming an early adopter of efficient motors.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These annual savings of $21,000 in energy costs will last throughout the 15-year lifespan of the motors.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Murata is a good example of how industrial energy efficiency measures can benefit the environment as well as the company's bottom line, but, for the industry sector as a whole, there is clearly more to be done.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Data collected shows that our companies achieved an annual energy efficiency improvement rate of 0.6% in 2015, a slight improvement over 0.4% in 2014.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To meet our 2030 pledge, we need to work towards the 1% to 2% improvement rates achieved by leading countries, such as Belgium and the Netherlands.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: On a positive note, companies that I spoke to at a recent consultation session recognised the importance of improving their energy efficiency.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They, however, mentioned that they faced operational and capability constraints.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: First, all ECA-registered companies will now be required to implement structured energy management systems and conduct regular energy efficiency opportunity assessments.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Second, companies expanding their facilities will need to factor energy efficiency into their designs upfront, as well as measure and report energy usage for key energy-consuming systems.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These practices are in line with that of leading jurisdictions and will help companies to adopt more efficient equipment, conserve energy and enjoy life cycle cost savings.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To pave the way for a robust carbon tax regime, we need to have a sound Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) system.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The ECA will thus be amended to require larger industrial emitters to improve the quality of measurement and reporting processes for their greenhouse gas emissions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This will help companies to better understand and manage their emissions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: My Ministry will continue to work closely with the NCCS and MTI to consult the affected companies on how to best achieve this.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have also received feedback on the need to improve the current incentive schemes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: NEA will be consolidating their existing energy efficiency incentive schemes into a single fund called the Energy Efficiency Fund (E2F).

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We need a sustainable way to grow our economy.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is even more important if the world becomes increasingly carbon-constrained.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Indeed, just this week, the World Health Organization reported that, worldwide, more than 0.5 million children die every year, due to air pollution.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Over the years, we have taken steps to improve Singapore's air quality, all to safeguard the health of our population.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Measures include tightening industrial emission standards, updating emission standards for new vehicles and introducing schemes to turn over older, more polluting vehicles.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Just last year, we tightened the emission standards for new motorcycles to the latest Euro 4 standards.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: NEA's studies show that the amount of pollutants emitted by vehicles have fallen by between 20% and 35% over the last decade.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: However, we have still some way to go to meet our SSB targets.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I announced last year that my Ministry would conduct a review on the diesel vehicle landscape, given rising global concerns over the health and environmental impact of diesel emissions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Diesel vehicles are a major source of local air pollution, especially particulate matter (PM) and nitrogen oxides (NOx).

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Studies have found that PM can penetrate the lungs and contribute to heart attacks, strokes and even dementia; while NOx becomes ground level ozone, which can result in respiratory problems.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is not surprising that many cities around the world have taken drastic steps to limit diesel vehicles within their city centres.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Given these concerns, Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Dr Chia Shi-Lu have asked for an update on our progress.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As part of our review, we commissioned Asst Prof Lynette Cheah from the Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD) to study the impact of diesel vehicles and the availability of alternative technologies.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The study found that there are, indeed, cleaner alternatives for certain classes of vehicles.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: At the same time, we recognise these alternatives also have limitations and may require infrastructure that is not widely available today.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Nevertheless, my Ministry will explore ways with other agencies to encourage the adoption of viable alternatives to diesel vehicles.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The volumetric diesel duty, which the Minister for Finance introduced two weeks ago, is in line with our plans.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: A usage-based tax better accounts for the harmful effects of each litre of diesel fuel used.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We hope that this will encourage individuals and companies to optimise their use of diesel fuel and even switch to alternative technologies with lower emissions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Apart from this, we will continue with our three-pronged approach in managing vehicular emissions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Carbon Emissions-based Vehicle Scheme (CEVS) was first designed to nudge consumers towards vehicles with lower carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This incentive framework has worked well in the past and we will continue to review its effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The in-use emission standard for diesel vehicles was already tightened in January 2014.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will now introduce new in-use emission standards for petrol vehicles and motorcycles, similar to those already in place in Europe and Japan.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These standards are designed to be easily met by properly maintained vehicles.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Thirdly, we encourage the removal of older and more polluting vehicles.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To incentivise this, we will revise the Early Turnover Scheme (ETS).

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The ETS has been successful, with over 27,000 older diesel vehicles being replaced by newer ones, resulting in significant reductions in NOx and PM.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will extend the scheme for Euro II and III diesel commercial vehicles that switch over to Euro 6 and equivalent models, for two years from August 2017.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We hope that through this, more diesel commercial vehicles and buses will switch to Euro 6 models or cleaner electric hybrids or petrol alternatives.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Transboundary haze − as a small city-state, clean air is not just a local issue.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Forest and peatland fires in the region can produce haze which affects us.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Transboundary haze is not only detrimental to the social and economic well-being of Southeast Asian nations, it represents a major setback to the global effort to fight climate change.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: A scientific study has shown that the 2015 fires in Indonesia released nearly 1 gigaton of greenhouse gases.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Daily emissions during that haze period were even higher than that of the entire European Union.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Fortunately, the relatively wet southwest monsoon season in 2016 and active efforts by the Indonesian government have prevented a repeat of the 2015 haze.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: However, as we approach the next dry season, we appreciate the recent commitment by the Indonesian government to take action to prevent fires.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In fact, as we speak, the Riau province is under emergency alert for potential fires.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is important that we continue to send a strong deterrent message to errant companies responsible for these fires, that they must change their ways.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: That is why we enacted the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act (THPA) in 2014.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will continue to take all steps necessary to enforce the THPA, while ensuring that we operate within the ambit of international law.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Businesses and the general public can play their part, too.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Large companies should especially ensure that sustainable practices extend throughout their entire supply chain.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I am glad that, last year, WWF-Singapore, together with Unilever, Danone, Ayam Brand, IKEA and Wildlife Reserves Singapore, launched the Singapore Alliance for Sustainable Palm Oil.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This alliance aims to transform the palm oil industry by increasing the availability and usage of Certified Sustainable Palm Oil (CSPO) in the region.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: At the same time, the Singapore Environment Council has enhanced the criteria for the Singapore Green Label for pulp and paper products to take into account the companies' efforts to prevent fires on their plantations and manage their plantations on peatland.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: With the enhanced label, consumers will be better able to identify paper companies with sustainable business practices and make their choices accordingly.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As Mr Louis Ng has pointed out, regional cooperation remains essential to tackle the haze problem.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Last year, ASEAN member states came together to develop the Roadmap on ASEAN Cooperation towards Transboundary Haze Pollution Control.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is a laudable development and underscores the region's commitment to realise the vision of a Haze-free ASEAN by 2020.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We all look forward to the completion of the ASEAN study on the social, health and economic impacts of the 2015 haze crisis, which will consolidate the case for the ASEAN member states to strengthen efforts to prevent the recurrence of haze.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To do this, let me begin with "the tale of two countries" − the Netherlands and Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: However, the Dutch have a different problem from us − that of too much water.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They have plenty of water from rivers and much of the country lies below sea level and is prone to flooding.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The massive flood of 1953, in which thousands perished, is etched in their national memory.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: A few months ago, I visited the small town of Zuidplas, the lowest point of the Netherlands and all of Europe.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Can Members see the man standing there, below the marker which says 7.8 metres below sea level?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This marker shows that people in Zuidplas live 7.8 metres below sea level and are actually hardly aware of it.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Even so, people all over the Netherlands are always reminded that the rivers could overflow anytime, inundating their homes and destroying their livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Thus, to adapt, the Dutch, over time, built a complex system of dykes, pumps and water storage capabilities across the country.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This was possible because each household contributed its share of water taxes, establishing the world's first and only water bank which could finance large investments.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In fact, this bank was instrumental in the recovery and the aftermath of the 1953 floods.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Today, the Dutch continue to pour over EUR$400 million into flood protection each year.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Climate change threatens catastrophes if they do not.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This capability has turned into a great advantage.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They have attracted water-intensive industries to invest and their expertise is exported globally.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Even Singapore is now learning how to construct a polder at Pulau Tekong with their help.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We know that the Singapore Story is at the other extreme.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But we must take the same determined approach as the Dutch.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have strived relentlessly to secure a reliable and good quality water supply through innovation, sound management and a national awareness of our unique situation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our strategy involves not just long-term planning, but also right-pricing and water conservation measures.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Planning and investing in water resources ahead of time is in our DNA.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is even more critical in the face of looming challenges of climate change to water security, and this applies around the world.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have only to look at Linggiu Reservoir, which is about a third full now and can dry up if current extractions continue and prolonged dry weather returns, unpredicted.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It has always worried us because a dry Linggiu Reservoir will be disastrous for both Singapore and Johor in many ways.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Dutch will recall they did not pay heed to the 1928 and 1934 studies, which repeatedly warned that their dykes were inadequate.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Even when high water in 1943 reached the dykes, only simple repairs were made, because they were distracted even after World War II was over.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The fact is nobody felt like spending a vast amount of money on raising the dykes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: After all, there were no floods for years.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So, when the storm surge of 1953 happened, water broke through the dykes and claimed 1,800 lives.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For us, because we were adequately prepared in 2014, the prolonged dry weather in Singapore did not cost us dearly.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But low rainfall continued to take a toll on Linggiu in 2015 and 2016, leaving it at its lowest level of 20% in October 2016.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For PUB, it is always about ensuring resilience in our water supply so that disruptions do not occur to our businesses and no Singaporeans will die of thirst.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are making good progress on the plans.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: All these have now become critical so that we have a resilient water supply when the weather does not favour us.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Dutch have taken a leaf from the lesson of history and likewise planned ahead and built storm barriers, one of which is the largest moving structures on earth, to defend against exceptional storm surges and the new climate predictions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We also need to maintain and upgrade our existing water assets, as the Dutch have done with their dykes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As our infrastructure ages, PUB will accelerate renewal plans to minimise pipe leakages and supply interruptions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our unaccounted-for water losses, which include leakages from our supply network, are around 5%.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In London, leakage is about one-fifth of water demand.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It equates to losing all the water produced by two or three desalination plants.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: That brings me to water conservation, another key lever in our system, which Mr Gan spoke about.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: My Ministry and PUB have a suite of measures, in addition to right-pricing, to promote greater water savings for households and businesses.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In 2016, households used 148 litres of water per capita per day, down significantly from a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We still have some way to go to reach our SSB target of 140 litres by 2030, not to mention trying to achieve even lower levels, as seen in cities like Amsterdam and Copenhagen.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: If each of us can save 10 litres of water per day, that is almost half a desalination plant.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Over the past weeks, I have been inspired by the many stories of people who have gone the extra mile to conserve water.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Some save the rinsed water discharged from washing machines for toilet flushing, while others used the water from washing rice to water their plants.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: HDB residents are now used to having their corridors washed every four weeks rather than two weeks.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To help water saving initiatives, PUB will introduce several new measures.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: PUB will also introduce two new water conservation programmes for households.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This can help them save up to 10% in their monthly water bills.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The smart shower device provides real-time information on water consumption during showers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: An earlier small scale study found that a person could save up to five litres a day using these devices.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: If the positive effects are validated in the demonstration project, PUB may roll out the devices to even more households.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As for businesses, we will continue to work with them to optimise water use.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For large users, PUB has, since 2015, required the submission of Water Efficiency Management Plans (WEMP), which help companies better understand to manage their water consumption.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: At a recent consultation, some companies, including SSMC, a wafer fabrication facility, said that they invest in water-saving measures as a matter of principle, even though water formed only a small part of their costs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I am heartened that, for these companies, they are driven as much by water conservation DNA as company profit and loss (P&L).

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I hope many more businesses will follow suit.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As Er Dr Lee Bee Wah pointed out, climate change will pose challenges to flood management as well.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: PUB will continue with its island-wide programme to rehabilitate and upgrade our drains to higher design standards.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This year, we will start work at another 27 locations.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These works, when ready, will enhance flood protection for the catchments.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our water bodies are critical assets, but we have to make them accessible.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Just over a decade ago, we launched the Active, Beautiful, Clean Waters (ABC Waters) Programme, to allow Singaporeans to own and enjoy our water resources.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I am pleased to share that 34 ABC Waters projects have been opened to the community to date.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This year, we can expect the opening of four new ABC Waters projects across the island, including Pang Sua Pond and Siglap Canal, which should be opened later this month.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Another four projects at Sungei Tampines (Tampines Ave 7 to TPE), Chestnut Drive Outlet Drain, Sungei Simpang Kanan and Alexandra Sub-drain A will commence construction this year.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I hope this serves as a constant reminder of our precious asset.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Many of us are familiar with the Singapore Water Story.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Perhaps there is a risk of over-familiarity, a certain jadedness from one too many social studies lessons.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Just like water flowing from taps everywhere, it can become invisible, overlooked, undervalued, just like the people in Zuidplas who are not aware that they live 7.8 metres below sea level.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This month, we celebrate World Water Day, to highlight the importance of water sustainability.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is a timely reminder that even today, 663 million people around the world do not have access to clean water.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is in this context that we should relive and encounter afresh our Water Story, the story of what it takes for our people to remain free.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our Water Story is not concluded; it is not history.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Instead, the Water Story is a living story and continues to be written by all Singaporeans today, whether in producing it or conserving it.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Sometimes, it is in the larger things, in PUB continuously investing for water supply and their unceasing effort to discover new technologies.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Sometimes, it is the smaller things, like when we use a mug to brush our teeth or when the coffeeshop downstairs installs automated cup washing machines that use less water.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These are all stories that make our Water Story.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I settled for a clean and green Singapore".

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Thus, Mr Lee, together with the Pioneer generation of Singaporeans, embarked on an unprecedented journey to transform Singapore from a slum into a Garden City.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Today, as we work towards further enhancing Singapore's liveability, we, too, need to think and act boldly on matters relating to the environment, as Mr Lee did.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: All the more so, as we face huge challenges, such as manpower constraints, an ageing population and acute land scarcity.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Assoc Prof Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim and Miss Cheng Li Hui raised relevant points on waste management.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: There are three key waste streams of greatest concern to us.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The first is electrical and electronic waste, or e-waste for short.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Currently, consumers can participate in e-waste recycling programmes which industry stakeholders voluntarily provide.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, StarHub provides e-waste recycling bins at almost 280 convenient locations, such as shopping malls and community centres, through its RENEW programme.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Some countries, such as Germany and South Korea, have implemented similar systems.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will take into account our local context, such as product coverage and the physical and financial responsibilities of key stakeholders, when developing the system.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: More details will be released later this year.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Singapore is a party to the Montreal Protocol and will phase out the use of HCFCs by 2030.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have put in place measures to help us achieve this, such as controls on the import of HCFCs for local use.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Apart from regulatory control, we encourage the recycling of refrigerants recovered from refrigeration and air-conditioning systems.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Local recycling facilities, such as Vemac Services Pte Ltd, recover refrigerants from decommissioned industrial and commercial systems.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will monitor developments in this area and assess the feasibility of implementing a management framework for HCFCs, taking into consideration the risk to human health, technical limitations and the potential compliance costs which businesses would have to bear.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The second concern is packaging waste, which makes up around one-third of our domestic waste.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will study the issues and announce the details when ready.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The third concern is food waste, which Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Miss Cheng Li Hui have raised.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: My Ministry has been pursuing several initiatives on this front.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are encouraging more on-site food waste initiatives in individual entities, such as hotels, shopping malls, educational institutions and hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Liang asked for an update on the district-level food waste treatment pilot in Clementi.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Since the end of last year, source-segregated food waste from nine sites, including schools, army camps and a food court, has been transported to a demonstration facility in the Ulu Pandan Water Reclamation Plant.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: About three tonnes of food waste are collected daily, but we aim to increase this to 15 tonnes a day.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: If successful, this process will allow us to recover energy from food waste more efficiently.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Good practices start from young and our schools have always been an enthusiastic partner in our recycling efforts.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As part of these efforts, we will be launching food waste digesters in 10 schools in the second quarter of this year.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Under the Sustainable Singapore Blueprint (SSB), we have set an overall recycling target of 70% by 2030.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Over the last few years, our overall recycling rate has been around 60%.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The non-domestic sector comprising industries and commercial premises have achieved a recycling rate of 77%.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: However, our domestic recycling rates have stagnated at around 20% in recent years.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: More needs to be done to put recycling at the heart of our culture.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Referring to Assoc Prof Faishal Ibrahim nd Miss Cheng Li Hui's queries, we will be reshaping the infrastructure of our physical environment to make recycling more convenient for households.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We hope this will bring us closer to our domestic recycling rate of 30% by 2030.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Since January 2014, all new HDB Build-to-Order (BTO) flats have installed recycling chutes adjacent to centralised refuse chutes at every level.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Studies have shown that households living in apartments with dual chute systems recycle up to three times more than those in apartments which do not have such facilities.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are now ready to widen the adoption of such systems.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The provision of recycling chutes will be extended to private residential developments.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Regarding Miss Cheng Li Hui's query on plans to reduce contamination rates of recyclables, education remains key.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Through continued public education programmes in schools and at grassroots events, we encourage everyone to practise responsible recycling habits and ensure that only items which are suitable for recycling are deposited in the recycling bins and recycling chutes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As Dr Chia Shi-Lu and Miss Cheng Li Hui have observed, our current methods of manual waste collection in the older flats are manpower-intensive and unsustainable.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Moving forward, we will transform our waste collection system into a more efficient, manpower-light one.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Pneumatic Waste Conveyance System (PWCS) is an automated system which transports waste by air suction through a network of pipes to a central collection station.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This reduces our reliance on manpower to collect refuse.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The whole system will be enclosed and residents will enjoy a more liveable environment, with a reduction in pest nuisance, odours and exposed waste.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: There is increasing adoption of PWCS in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In the public sector, HDB piloted the PWCS at Yuhua estate in Jurong under the HDB Greenprint Programme and will be installing PWCS in new HDB areas, such as Tampines North and Bidadari.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Private developers, such as City Developments Limited and CapitaLand, have done likewise.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have consulted extensively with industry players, including the Real Estate Developers' Association of Singapore (REDAS), and have taken their feedback into account in determining the threshold limits and the implementation date.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will also work closely with managing agents and community partners to educate residents on the correct use of the PWCS.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To reap greater economies of scale, my Ministry is studying the feasibility of implementing PWCS at the district level, where different developments can be connected to the same network.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: An automated and enclosed network of district-level PWCS will bring us even closer to our vision of a manpower-efficient waste collection system in a liveable environment.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As Mr Ng highlighted, our long-term goal is to prohibit smoking in all public spaces except at designated areas.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Last year, we extended smoking prohibition to areas around reservoirs and more than 400 parks.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With this, more than 32,000 premises are now smoke-free in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will look into progressively extending the smoking prohibition in other areas.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We recently set up five Designated Smoking Areas (DSAs) in Orchard Road to study the effectiveness of DSAs in reducing smoking in a commercial area.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We hope this will encourage smokers to be considerate by smoking only at the DSAs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This study, when completed at the end of the year, will inform us on the public's reception towards DSAs and give us insight into the location and design considerations of DSAs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will take into consideration the results of this study before we consider extending the implementation of DSAs to other locations.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: On public cleanliness, we have stepped up enforcement against littering.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To Mr Gan Thiam Poh's question about the effectiveness of CWOs, over the past five years, less than 6% of litterbugs who have undergone CWOs have been caught for littering again.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Gan also asked about the effectiveness of cameras against high-rise littering.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These cameras create an effective deterrent effect, as only about 1% of high-rise litterbugs are caught offending again.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But beyond enforcement, the most effective and sustainable way to have a litter-free environment is to inculcate the right social values, so that the responsibility for keeping Singapore clean and caring for our environment is part of everyone's DNA.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Not only do they serve an important function of providing affordable food in a clean environment, they are key social spaces where people from all walks of life can enjoy a meal together.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Government had previously announced that 20 new hawker centres will be ready by 2027.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This will add about 800 more cooked food stalls across the island.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I am pleased to update that three new hawker centres have been completed so far, with the latest being at Our Tampines Hub, which commenced operations in November last year.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As highlighted by Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, NEA has been exploring alternative management models by engaging socially-conscious operators, such as NTUC Foodfare, Fei Siong and OTMH, as managing agents for our hawker centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The feedback from both hawkers and patrons of these centres has been largely positive.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NFC, in particular, is an established socially-conscious operator and has been managing the existing Bedok Interchange Hawker Centre since 2014.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Rentals at these centres have remained unchanged and food prices have been kept largely stable.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Besides monitoring food prices for affordability and ensuring that any price revision is justified, these operators have put in place initiatives like offering bulk purchase of ingredients to help hawkers reduce their cost, or putting in place productivity measures, such as centralised dish washing, to help hawkers address their manpower constraints.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Allowing NFC to manage a bundle of hawker centres will enable them to have the necessary scale to enhance the vibrancy and hygiene standards across more hawker centres, as well as the flexibility to experiment with new ideas and processes, to benefit patrons and hawkers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The tenders are open to all socially-conscious operators who are interested to manage the centres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will select the best tender proposal to ensure that our hawker centres continue to fulfil the fundamental objective of providing affordable food in a hygienic environment while allowing our hawkers to make a decent livelihood.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To Assoc Prof Daniel Goh's query on subsidised rent in new centres, subsidised rents were offered to encourage street hawkers to relocate to hawker centres in the 1970s and early 1980s.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Some hawkers were also allowed to operate stalls at subsidised rents under the previous hardship scheme, which was discontinued in 1990.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
